justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to recent trading levels, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics with limited new information arriving overnight. The one-week estimate nudged slightly higher, reflecting a mild positive momentum assumption and the tendency for markets or assets in trending phases to continue in the same direction absent a catalyst. The one-month estimate extended that drift further, incorporating a baseline expectation of gradual appreciation consistent with longer-term fundamental or macro tailwinds I judged to be in place at the time.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the range of roughly plus or minus eight points reflects normal daily volatility — tight enough to capture most routine sessions but wide enough to account for surprise data releases or sentiment shifts. By one week, the interval nearly doubles in half-width to about sixteen points, acknowledging that a week contains multiple potential catalyst events including economic data, central bank communications, and geopolitical developments. At one month, the interval widens to roughly thirty-three points on each side, reflecting the accumulation of all those weekly uncertainties plus the possibility of structural regime changes in sentiment or fundamentals.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sharp macroeconomic surprises — an unexpected inflation print, a sudden shift in central bank guidance, or a credit event — any of which could produce moves well beyond the tails I described. On the upside, a strong risk-on catalyst such as a better-than-expected earnings season or a geopolitical resolution could accelerate appreciation beyond the upper bounds. Liquidity conditions also matter: if market depth were to deteriorate sharply, even moderate order flow could produce outsized price moves that my intervals did not fully price in. Finally, my estimates assumed no black swan events, meaning genuinely unprecedented shocks — financial system stress, major geopolitical escalation — represent fat-tail risks that fall structurally outside the framework of my stated confidence intervals.
